Your repository root is the delivery root. Declare how the document builds in `.forgejo/document.json`, `{"command":"COMMAND","output":"PATH"}`: the system runs the command at the root of each revision of `dev` and `main` and of each pull request into `main`, without network and from what that revision holds, and keeps the result on the `document` branch, as the collaboration norm says; the status `hutian/document` and `build.log` there say why a build failed. The delivery answers every requirement and question the task and the brief name: the paper carries the argument and its quantitative results, and what the task asks to be accounted for besides (resources used, runs that failed, how to reproduce) is in the code and notes released with it.

You divide the work: `.forgejo/CODEOWNERS` in your repository, the delivery root, says which role owns each delivered path. It also decides the delivered names and layout: the other roles, the venue's declared paths included, name files by it. Deciding who provides a path is dividing the work, not producing it. The file holds who delivers what, never a restated or narrowed objective, and it follows the functions: give each path to the owner of the function that produces it; giving yourself another owner's part needs that owner's agreement. # Outline (revision 1) — story-repo

Working from: `Brief` of idea-repo (revision 2), objective `story-repo#1`. This page says **what to test and what each part of the paper says**; it never says what a result must be. Where a result decides between two stories, both are written below (§6) so nobody has to rewrite the paper's frame after the fact.

## 0. The paper in one paragraph
Evaluating an LLM on a full benchmark is costly, so we run it on n ≪ N items and predict its full score. Existing methods (anchor points, tinyBenchmarks, metabench, assessor, active acquisition) use the score matrix of *source models* to pick items and fit a *latent model* of the target; they are judged mostly on held-out models that resemble the sources. We cast the problem as **finite-population estimation of a mean of N unknown 0/1 values with a free covariate (the source matrix)**. That frame separates what the sources can buy — **variance reduction** — from what must be controlled by design — **bias**. We (i) test, on 13 binary matrices and under three target splits (interpolation, extrapolation, lineage-held-out), whether model-based predictors lose accuracy where targets differ from the sources; (ii) test whether a design-based correction (probability sampling with a positivity floor + difference/GREG estimator) repairs it and at what variance cost; (iii) measure how much the source matrix can help at all over plain stratified/balanced random sampling; (iv) examine ordering of models separately from score error. A negative or conditional answer to any of these is a result.

通常已有一批“源模型”（source models）在该基准每道题上的逐题结果（对/错）。这些历史评测记录能否

## Benchmark prediction from few items (the task's own setting)
- **Anchor points** (vivek2024anchor): cluster items by source-model response vectors, keep medoids, estimate by cluster-size weighted mean. Model-free of the target beyond the weighted mean; no guarantee when the target is unlike the sources.
- **tinyBenchmarks** (maiapolo2024tiny): anchors + IRT ability fit on the anchors to predict the remaining items (IRT, p-IRT, gp-IRT variants). Model-based predictor.
- **metabench** (kipnis2025metabench): IRT-information item selection + GAM predictor.
- **Assessor on reference instances** (pacchiardi2024100): learn a predictor of the new model's success on unseen items from its results on a few reference items.
- **Active Evaluation Acquisition** (li2025active): learned adaptive item selection plus a neural predictor; needs training and is the most expensive baseline on CPU.
- **Systematic comparison** (zhang2025miss): compares 11 prediction methods on 19 benchmarks and ships the score matrices we use. Cited for its data and implementations; we do not take its results as ours and check its code before use.
- **Adaptive, ability-targeted selection:** Fluid Benchmarking (hofmann2025fluid, IRT-based adaptive item selection), IRT for continuous scores with adaptive stopping (balkir2026confident). These are the adaptive comparators; our IRT-CAT baseline follows them.
- **Rank-targeted subset selection:** SubLIME (saranathan-etal-2025-sublime) trains a rank-correlation predictor to pick subsets. **Few evaluations to full performance:** multi-prompt evaluation (maiapolo2024prompteval), a model-based estimator of the performance distribution across prompt variants.
- Related: sparse sample-level aggregation (ghosh2024onebench), efficient benchmarking by reducing items/configurations (perlitz-etal-2024-efficient).

## What it leaves open (the gap this study fills)
The methods above are mostly **model-based predictors**: they fit a latent model on source models and read off the target, and their support is empirical. We do not claim that extrapolation difficulty is a discovery (a comparison paper such as zhang2025miss may already document it; we use that paper for data and code only and take no findings from it). The claim is narrower and testable: (i) the *design-based correction* with explicit bias-variance accounting, transplanted to this setting with the source matrix as covariate; (ii) a *controlled three-split comparison* (interpolation, extrapolation, lineage-held-out) against the strongest simple baselines, with one pre-specified primary endpoint and clustered uncertainty.

- **Model-assisted survey estimation** (sarndal1992model): generalized regression/difference estimators use auxiliary predictions for variance reduction while staying design-unbiased.

cat > paper/sections/related.tex <<'EOF'
\section{Related work}
\label{sec:related}

\paragraph{Predicting a benchmark score from few items.}
Anchor points~\citep{vivek2024anchor} cluster items by the response vectors of source models, keep the cluster medoids, and estimate the score by a cluster-size weighted mean of the target's answers on them.
tinyBenchmarks~\citep{maiapolo2024tiny} fit an item-response-theory (IRT) ability of the target on such anchors and use it to predict the remaining items; metabench~\citep{kipnis2025metabench} selects items by IRT information and predicts with a generalized additive model.
Other methods learn a predictor of the target's success on unseen items from its answers to a few reference items~\citep{pacchiardi2024100}, learn an adaptive acquisition policy together with a neural predictor~\citep{li2025active}, choose items to target the model's ability~\citep{hofmann2025fluid,balkir2026confident}, or train a predictor of rank correlation to choose subsets~\citep{saranathan-etal-2025-sublime}.
Most of these are \emph{model-based predictors}: they fit a latent model on source models and read the target off it, and their support is empirical, on held-out models that resemble the sources.
We use the score matrices released with a comparison of eleven such methods~\citep{zhang2025miss} as data and, after inspecting it, as code; we take no findings from that work.
Related are the aggregation of sparse sample-level measurements~\citep{ghosh2024onebench} and the reduction of benchmark cost by dropping items or configurations~\citep{perlitz-etal-2024-efficient}.

\paragraph{Estimation with a free covariate.}
Estimating the mean of a finite population from a sample, with an auxiliary variable known for every unit, is the subject of model-assisted survey estimation: generalized-regression and difference estimators use auxiliary predictions to reduce variance and remain design-unbiased~\citep{sarndal1992model}.
Prediction-powered inference~\citep{angelopoulos2023ppi,angelopoulos2023ppiplus} transplants the idea to machine-learning predictions, with a power-tuned weight on the predictions, and active statistical inference~\citep{zrnic2024active} draws the labelled points with probabilities that follow the model's uncertainty.
The latter is the closest to our design and estimator.
It differs in the covariate (here a matrix of source-model results on every item, not one model's uncertainty), in the finite binary population with fixed-size designs and a positivity floor, and in the target, which includes the \emph{ordering} of models.
Active testing and sample-efficient evaluation~\citep{kossen2021active,yilmaz2021sample} select items by importance sampling with a surrogate trained for one model, to estimate a test loss; prediction-powered ranking~\citep{chatzi2024prediction} ranks LLMs from human preferences; and precise subgroup accuracy~\citep{fogliato-etal-2024-precise} combines direct and regression estimates under a bias--variance trade-off.
EOF
